On the first evening in his own house, Waythorn stood on the drawing room hearth and waited for his new wife to come down to dinner. <break time="0.8s" /> They had been hastily recalled from their honeymoon by the illness of Lily Haskett, the child of Missus Waythorns first marriage, who had come down with typhoid fever. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, however, the doctor reported that the child was out of danger, and Waythorn felt a deep sense of peace as he looked around the softly lit room. <break time="0.8s" /> When Alice came down at last, she looked so fresh and serene that no one would have guessed she had spent anxious nights beside a sick child. <break time="0.8s" /> After dinner she told him, with some hesitation, that Lilys father had written through his lawyer to ask whether he might see his daughter. <break time="0.8s" /> Under the courts decree Haskett was entitled to see the child at regular times, and Waythorn, though he disliked the idea, admitted that the visits could not be refused. <break time="0.8s" /> Alice had divorced two husbands before she married Waythorn, first a man named Haskett and then Gus Varick, a well known figure in New York society. <break time="0.8s" /> Her two divorces had given people plenty to gossip about, but Waythorn was convinced that she had been unlucky rather than wrong, and he did not regret his choice. <break time="0.8s" /> Seldom had he felt so certain of his happiness as he did that evening, sitting by the fire with his wife and believing that the past was finally behind them.
